heading: INT. HARTWIG OBSERVATORY - DOME CHAMBER - NIGHT

units.text: INT. HARTWIG OBSERVATORY - DOME CHAMBER - NIGHT
A great brass telescope tilts toward a slit of stars.
Star charts blanket every wall.
A desk lamp, a cold teapot, a black intercom box on the wall.
PROFESSOR EMIL HARTWIG, 60s, rumpled tweed, ink on his cuffs, sits hunched over a ledger.
He looks up at the intercom as it crackles.
Professor? Are you still up there?
units.name: CORA

units.text: Who is that?
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: The night porter's niece. They let me in at the gate. I need to ask you about the Calloway disappearance.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Hartwig closes the ledger very carefully.
I don't discuss that. Good night.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: Your assistant was last seen climbing these stairs. Eleven years ago tonight.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Is that what the papers say?
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: That is what the logbook says. The one in your hand.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Hartwig's fingers tighten on the ledger.
He glances at the dome door.
The door at the bottom is locked.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: I know. I'm calling from the landing.
units.name: CORA

units.text: A knock, three soft raps, echoes up the iron staircase.
Hartwig stands.
His chair scrapes.
How did you get a key?
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: I didn't. It was never locked from my side.
units.name: CORA

units.text: The dome door swings open.
CORA BELLINGHAM, 30s, rain-soaked trench coat, a brass key on a chain around her neck, steps into the lamplight.
She holds a small handset against her ear and clicks it off.
Hello, Professor.
units.name: CORA

units.text: You're not the porter's niece.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: No.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Then who?
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: Daniel Calloway was my brother.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Hartwig takes a step back and bumps the telescope.
It swings an inch and groans.
I was cleared. There was an inquiry.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: There was. It asked the wrong questions.
units.name: CORA

units.text: She walks to the desk and puts the brass key on the ledger.
That's the key to the sub-basement. Daniel's key. It was in his coat, in the river.
units.name: CORA

units.text: That proves nothing.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: It proves he had a reason to go down there. Why would an astronomer go down?
units.name: CORA

units.text: Cora--
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: You said my name. I didn't give it.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Hartwig stops.
The lamp hums.
A moth circles it.
Heard it from the porter. At the gate.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: The porter retired in March.
units.name: CORA

units.text: Silence.
Hartwig sits slowly in his chair.
He fell, you understand. There was an instrument case on the stair. A terrible accident.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: Then why hide it?
units.name: CORA

units.text: Because he wasn't alone on the stair.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: He opens the ledger and turns it toward her.
A page of neat handwriting, and below it a second hand, shakier.
Read the last line. Not mine.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: Cora leans over the page.
Her face does not change, but her hand finds the edge of the desk.
"I pushed him. Forgive me. - T. Wexler."
units.name: CORA

units.text: The old director. He died that winter. I've kept this page for eleven years, because I didn't know who to hand it to.
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: You could have handed it to the police.
units.name: CORA

units.text: And be asked why I waited?
units.name: HARTWIG

units.text: Yes. Why did you wait?
units.name: CORA

units.text: Hartwig looks up at the slit of sky, where a single bright star hangs.
Because I was afraid he would come back and ask me the same thing.
units.name: HARTWIG
